title: Fewest Buses Between Stops
statement:
A city has several bus lines. routes[i] lists the stops bus i visits; each bus drives its loop forever, so once you are on bus i you can ride to any of its stops. You can change buses at any stop two lines share.

You start at stop source (not on any bus yet) and want to reach stop target. Return the fewest number of buses you have to board, or -1 if it cannot be done. If source equals target, the answer is 0.

What counts is buses boarded, not stops passed.

examples.why: Bus 0 takes you to 5 or 8, and from either you need one more bus to reach 11. No single bus serves both 2 and 11.
Six stops apart, but one bus. Counting stops (BFS over stops with one step per stop) gets this wrong.
The two lines share no stop, so you can never change from one to the other.

constraints: 1 ≤ routes[i].length, and the total number of stops over all routes is at most 100 000
The stops of one route are distinct
hints: BFS over stops with one step per stop measures the wrong thing. What should one step of the search be?
Make the buses the nodes: one BFS step = boarding one more bus. Two buses are connected if they share a stop. You need a map from each stop to the buses that serve it.

Start the BFS with every bus that serves source (that is 1 bus). When you process a bus, check whether it serves target; otherwise, for each of its stops, enqueue every unvisited bus through that stop. Mark stops as done too, so each stop's bus list is scanned once.

explain.intuition:
The cost is "buses boarded", so the search must count buses, not stops. Riding a bus to any of its stops is free; only switching costs one. That means each BFS layer should be "everything reachable with one more bus". Use the buses as graph nodes and connect two buses when they share a stop.

Building that bus graph explicitly can be slow, but you do not need to. Keep a map stop → buses. When you expand a bus, walk its stops, and for each stop look up the buses passing through it. Mark each stop as expanded the first time, so its list is never walked twice. Then every stop and every bus is touched a constant number of times, and the BFS is linear in the total route length.
steps: Build stopToBuses: for every route i and every stop s on it, add i to the list for s.
Put every bus serving source in the queue with distance 1, marking them visited, and mark source as an expanded stop.
Pop a bus. If any of its stops is target, return its distance. Otherwise for each of its stops not yet expanded, mark it and enqueue every unvisited bus in stopToBuses[stop] with distance + 1.
pitfalls: BFS over stops where every stop on a route is an edge from every other. It counts stops instead of buses and builds a quadratic number of edges for long routes.
Returning −1 when source equals target but is not on any route. Staying put needs no bus.
Not marking stops as expanded. A stop shared by many buses then gets its bus list scanned once per bus, which is quadratic on busy hubs.

solutions.title: BFS over stops with every ride as an edge
solutions.idea: Connect every pair of stops on the same route, then BFS from source. Each edge is one bus ride. Correct, but the edge count is quadratic in route length.

solutions.title: BFS over buses
solutions.idea: Each BFS layer is one more bus boarded. A stop-to-buses map finds the next buses, and each stop is expanded only once.

followups: Each bus has a fare and you want the cheapest trip instead of the fewest buses. What replaces BFS?
Return the actual sequence of buses to take, not just how many.
